title: The Judges of the Diaspora
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: This designation refers to Karna in [Sanhedrin 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.17b.5). It also appears in [Bava Batra 51a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.51a.1), [70a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.70a.1), [70b](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.70b.2) and [100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Bava_Batra.100a.10). Hyman reports that Rashbam (see [Rashbam on 51a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashbam_on_Bava_Batra.51a.1.1)) explains in all these places that the judges were Shmuel and Karna, citing [Sanhedrin 17b](https://www.sefaria.org/Sanhedrin.17b.5); Hyman concludes that this was undoubtedly his reading there. Hyman argues that although that passage calls Rav and Shmuel “our Rabbis in Babylonia,” this refers to the period after Rav Shila’s death, when they founded two academies and were called “our Rabbis in Babylonia.” Before that, Shmuel and Karna were simply “the judges of the Diaspora.” He considers this clear.[^1]

notes.text: The consulted Sanhedrin gives Karna and names Rav and Shmuel as “our Rabbis in Babylonia.” Rashbam gives Shmuel and Karna in his comments on [70a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashbam_on_Bava_Batra.70a.1.1), [70b](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashbam_on_Bava_Batra.70b.2.2) and [100a](https://www.sefaria.org/Rashbam_on_Bava_Batra.100a.10.2) as well. [Seder HaDorot](https://www.girsology.com/seder-hadorot.html?entry=928&lang=en) takes this as a mistake, while Hyman argues Rashbam had a different reading and explains the titles through the history of the academies.
